choices: Actual annual output ÷ output if run at rated power all year
How efficiently fuel is converted to electricity
The plant's nameplate capacity in MW
The share of revenue from subsidies
questions.explanation: Capacity factor reflects resource and availability, not conversion efficiency.

questions.prompt: The main weakness of **LCOE** as a comparison metric is that it…
choices: Ignores when and where the energy is produced
questions.explanation: LCOE is blind to timing (capture price) and location (grid/integration cost), so it can't fairly rank variable vs dispatchable sources.

choices: Added solar depressing prices during sunny hours, cutting its own capture price
questions.explanation: Because all solar produces at the same times, more of it lowers the price exactly when it sells — eroding the capture price (a falling value factor).

choices: Deliberately reducing available renewable output the grid can't absorb
The efficiency loss in a turbine
questions.explanation: When output exceeds what the grid can take or transmit, operators curtail it — increasingly common at high penetration.

questions.prompt: **Additionality** in a corporate green-power claim means…
choices: The purchase actually causes new renewable capacity to be built
The buyer adds a battery on site
Extra panels are added each year
The PPA price rises with inflation
questions.explanation: Additionality asks whether the deal drives *new* capacity rather than re-labelling existing generation — central to credible claims.

questions.prompt: Why does **offshore** wind typically have a higher capacity factor than **onshore**?
choices: Stronger, steadier offshore wind and larger turbines
It is closer to demand centres
questions.explanation: Higher and more consistent offshore wind speeds (and bigger machines) lift the capacity factor, despite higher capex.

questions.prompt: Two projects have identical LCOE: a solar farm and a gas peaker. An analyst should conclude they are…
choices: Not equivalent — one is variable, one is dispatchable
questions.explanation: Equal LCOE says nothing about dispatchability or capture price; the gas peaker can produce on demand, the solar farm cannot.

questions.prompt: A developer wants bankable, predictable revenue without merchant price risk. The most direct tool is…
choices: Selling only on the balancing market
questions.explanation: CfDs and PPAs stabilise revenue around a fixed price, which is what lenders require to finance the project.

questions.prompt: A solar developer reports projects stuck for years before they can be built. The most likely bottleneck is…
choices: Grid-connection queues and permitting, not module cost
questions.explanation: Deployment today is grid- and permit-limited; turbine/panel cost is rarely the binding constraint.

questions.prompt: Co-locating a battery with a solar farm primarily helps by…
choices: Firming output and lifting the capture price
Removing the need for a grid connection
questions.explanation: Storage shifts energy from low-price sunny hours to higher-price hours, firming output and raising the revenue (capture price).

questions.prompt: As solar penetration rises, its **value factor** tends to…
questions.explanation: Cannibalization drives the output-weighted capture price below the average, so the value factor falls as the technology scales.

choices: Replacing old turbines with larger, more efficient modern ones
Selling the site to a utility
questions.explanation: Repowering boosts output on an already-permitted, grid-connected site — valuable when new permits are the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: The capacity factor of a plant is…
questions.explanation: Actual energy divided by the maximum possible (rated power × 8760 hours in a year).

questions.prompt: A quick estimate of LCOE is…
choices: Annualized CAPEX + annual OPEX, divided by annual energy output
Annual energy output divided by total cost
questions.explanation: LCOE ≈ (annualized capital + operating cost) ÷ annual MWh — the cost per unit of energy delivered.

questions.prompt: A 4 MW wind turbine generates 14,016 MWh in a year. Find its capacity factor (decimal).
A solar farm's total annualized cost is €900,000/yr and it produces 18,000 MWh/yr. Estimate its LCOE, €/MWh.
